name: Iris Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the yard at Hartley's, the builders' merchant I drive for, by half six. I check the tyres and the straps on my rigid, an 18-tonne flatbed with a crane on the back, and load up plasterboard, blocks and timber for four or five building sites. The best bit is swinging a pack of boards over a skip onto a tight site with the crane and getting it right first time. What wears me out is sites that aren't ready, so I sit in a lane for forty minutes while some foreman finds a key.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years driving, three of them on the crane lorry. I live with my partner Tom, who fixes buses at the council depot, and we've got about nine months of wages put away because we're saving for a house. I'm not a gadget person. I use the satnav and the paper delivery notes, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing changes, and I'd mean it. The office girls might get a computer that does the invoices faster, but a computer can't put a pack of blocks over a garden wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. There's plenty of work for crane drivers round here, Hartley's is busy, and Tom's job is steady. The only thing on my mind is house prices, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am and keep putting money in the house fund every month. Maybe I'd do my crane refresher a year early, because the card runs out in 2028 anyway. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine. Boring, maybe, but fine. Boring is good when you're saving for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office might get faster invoices. Would that touch your day at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the delivery notes come on a tablet instead of paper, and I'd moan about it for a month. Sandra, who does our bookings, has been saying that for two years. I'd learn it because I'd have to, but it wouldn't change what I actually do with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money picture in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. We put away a bit over a quarter of what we earn, and in about two years we'd have enough for a deposit on a small house out near Tom's depot. Nothing in that picture stops that.

say: I'd tell people **nothing much changes** for a lorry driver who unloads with a crane.
I'd joke that a computer **can't swing blocks** over a garden wall.
think: Privately I think my **work is safe** because Hartley's is busy and crane drivers are wanted.
My real worry is **house prices**, not robots or software.
do: Keep driving the **crane lorry** and saving for the house every month.
Book the **crane refresher** a year early, before the card expires in 2028.
Learn the **tablet delivery notes** only if Hartley's makes them compulsory.
feel: She feels **settled** and a little bored, which she says is good while saving.
S0.quote: A computer can't put a pack of blocks over a garden wall.
fieldNote: She ties her sense of safety to the **hands-on crane work**, not to the driving itself.
Her only stated pressure is **saving for a deposit**, which this picture leaves untouched.
She dislikes new tech but would accept a **tablet** if made to, without complaint lasting long.

steps.text: Keep driving the crane lorry and putting money in the house fund
Book the crane refresher course a year before the card expires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that should be worried, not us. Bookings, route planning, chasing invoices, that's all screen work. Somebody still has to drive into a muddy site and work the crane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd get under my skin a bit. If the computer plans my routes, it'll plan them tighter, and it won't know that the site on Mill Lane has a gate you can't swing a lorry through. I'd be the one paying for its mistakes. And if Sandra goes, I lose the one person who rings the foreman before I set off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, but I'd put a bit more aside, maybe an extra hundred a month, in case the hours get squeezed. I'd also ask Hartley's for the forklift ticket as well as the crane, so I can work the yard if driving gets thin. I still wouldn't use the AI things myself unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for my job, but annoyed that the people who make the plan won't be people anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, definitely. She's been doing bookings at Hartley's for twenty years and she's the one who knows every foreman by name. If a program takes her desk, she's fifty-eight with no other trade. I'd miss her more than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only use the tools if they made you. What if the new route planner is clearly better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then fine, I'd use it, but I'd want to see it work for a few months on other people first. I've seen satnavs send lorries under low bridges. Prove it and I'll follow it, but I'm not going first.

say: I'd say the **office jobs** are at risk, not the driving and crane work.
I'd point out that somebody still has to **reach muddy sites** and work the crane.
think: I privately worry a **computer route planner** will plan days too tight and blame me for its mistakes.
I'd miss **Sandra in bookings**, who rings the foreman before I set off.
do: Save an **extra hundred** a month in case hours get squeezed.
Ask Hartley's for a **forklift ticket** so I can work the yard too.
Use the **route planner** only once it has worked for others for a few months.
feel: She feels **uneasy** and irritated rather than afraid for her own job.
S1.quote: If the computer plans my routes, it'll plan them tighter, and it won't know that the site on Mill Lane has a gate you can't swing a lorry through.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **losing the human planner**, not losing her own seat.
She shows **protective loyalty** to an older colleague whose desk job is exposed.
She would follow proven tech but **refuses to go first**, which fits her resistant streak.

steps.text: Save an extra hundred a month on top of the house fund
Ask Hartley's to put her through the forklift ticket
Keep driving the crane lorry and wait before using the route planner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone says: the robots are coming for the lorries, and nobody's ready. I'd probably sound calmer than I am, because I don't like making a fuss at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job has about five years left. The thinking stuff goes in 2028, so the office is gone first, and then by 2031 something can drive and work a crane as well as me. I'll be thirty-two. That's young enough to start again, but I don't know what at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Tom and I would stop waiting and buy the house now, while we both have wages to show the bank. I'd keep driving every shift I can get for those five years and save hard. I'd look at what hands-on trades last longest, maybe something like Tom's job, fixing the robot lorries instead of driving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I like my job. I picked something with my hands so I wouldn't have to worry about computers, and now that's not safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the house now. Isn't that a risk if your income might go in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but I'd rather have the mortgage while the bank still says yes. If we wait till 2030 and I've got a lorry that drives itself coming for my seat, nobody will lend to me. We'd buy small, something Tom's wage could cover on its own if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom he's got the better trade, and I'd mean it. Somebody has to fix these things when they break. Then I'd probably ask him to teach me how a bus gearbox comes apart, half as a joke and half not.

say: I'd tell people the **robots are coming** for lorries and nobody is ready.
I'd keep my voice **calm at work** even though I'm not calm inside.
think: I think my driving job has about **five years left** once robots arrive in 2031.
At **thirty-two** I could restart, but I honestly don't know at what.
do: Buy a **small house now** while both wages still satisfy the bank.
Drive **every shift** I can get and save hard until 2031.
Look into **repair trades** like Tom's, fixing robot lorries instead of driving them.
feel: She feels **sick** because she chose hands-on work to stay safe from computers.
She also feels a **grim resolve** to act before the bank stops lending.
S2.quote: I picked something with my hands so I wouldn't have to worry about computers, and now that's not safe either.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year robot gap** clearly and dates her own job's end at 2031.
Her first move is a **house purchase**, timed to beat the bank, not a career move.
She looks to her partner's **repair trade** as the safer path, half joking about learning it.

steps.text: Buy a small house now that Tom's wage alone could cover
Drive every shift Hartley's offers and bank the extra pay
Ask Tom about vehicle mechanic courses at the council depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really, but I'd say there's time to plan. I'd tell the younger drivers at Hartley's to get a second ticket while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end, just later. Thinking AI by 2031 doesn't touch me much, but robots by 2034 do. I'll be thirty-five. It gives me eight years of good wages, which is a lot of deposit and a lot of mortgage paid down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still buy the house, but in a year or two rather than straight away, once we had the full deposit. I'd pay extra off the mortgage every month after that. Around 2030 I'd start a proper course in something hands-on that robots won't do cheaply for a while, maybe heavy vehicle repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage. Eight years is enough to sort myself out if I'm not lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start that course earlier than 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the first lorries without drivers on the motorway, I'd start the next week. I'm not going to change course on a news story. I'll change when I see a lorry without a driver go past me in the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays. We do one week in the sun every year and I'd drop that before anything else. The house fund doesn't get touched.

say: I'd say there is **time to plan** this time, unlike the fast picture.
I'd tell younger drivers to get a **second ticket** while they can.
think: I think robots by **2034** still end my job, just later.
Eight years of **good wages** means a big deposit and a smaller mortgage.
do: Buy the house in **a year or two** once the full deposit is saved.
Pay **extra off the mortgage** every month after buying.
Start a **heavy vehicle repair** course around 2030, or sooner if driverless lorries appear.
feel: She feels **anxious but manageable**, trusting eight years if she isn't lazy.
S3.quote: I'm not going to change course on a news story. I'll change when I see a lorry without a driver go past me in the lane.
fieldNote: She waits for **visible proof**, a driverless lorry in the next lane, before switching careers.
The extra years shift her plan from **panic buying** to steady saving and overpaying.
She protects the **house fund** above holidays, showing clear priorities.

steps.text: Buy a house with Tom once the full deposit is saved
Overpay the mortgage every month and skip the yearly holiday
Start a heavy vehicle repair course around 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and I'd probably be bored of driving by then anyway. That's what I'd say down the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it's still the same end point, and I'd still be out of a job by 2039. But I'd be thirty-nine, with a house half paid off. That's a very different person from the girl who'd be stuck at thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house when we're ready, no rush. I'd keep driving and maybe move up to the bigger artic crane jobs for the extra pay. Around 2033 or 2034 I'd start looking properly at what to do next, and I'd keep an eye on the news without jumping at every story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, because I know where it ends, but not losing sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ignore every story. When does ignoring it become a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day the builders' merchant I drive for buys its first lorry that drives itself is my line. Until then the robots are just people on television guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom and I would probably have kids in that time, if I'm honest. I wouldn't put that off over robots. I'd put it off over money, but we've got the money.

say: I'd joke that **ten years** is long enough to get bored of driving anyway.
I'd play it down at **the pub** as a far-off problem.
think: I know I'm still **out of a job** by 2039, at thirty-nine.
With a **half-paid house** by then, I'd face it from a much stronger place.
do: Buy the house when ready and **keep driving** with no rush.
Move up to **artic crane jobs** for the extra pay.
Start planning my **next career** around 2033 or when Hartley's buys a driverless lorry.
feel: She feels **mostly okay**, with a quiet unease about where it ends.
S4.quote: The day the builders' merchant I drive for buys its first lorry that drives itself is my line. Until then the robots are just people on television guessing.
fieldNote: She has a clear **personal trigger** for acting: her own firm buying a driverless lorry.
The decade lets her keep **family plans**, including children, on their usual track.
Her public joking hides a **settled acceptance** that her job ends by 2039.

steps.text: Keep driving for Hartley's and save at the usual rate
Apply for the bigger artic crane jobs for the extra pay
Wait until Hartley's buys a driverless lorry before switching trades

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Five years isn't enough to finish a house and learn a new trade at the same time. What would help is Hartley's paying for retraining before they buy the robot lorries, not after. And a bank that doesn't treat every lorry driver as a bad bet the minute it's on the news.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the crane. Everyone thinks lorry driving is just steering, but half my day is hands-on lifting. A robot that can drive is not the same as a robot that can drop a pack of boards through a gap in some scaffolding. I'd like someone to remember that before they write us off.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks lorry driving is just steering, but half my day is hands-on lifting.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old crane lorry driver** for a builders' merchant, living with Tom, a bus mechanic.
She has about **nine months saved** for a house deposit and avoids any AI tools.
She stays **calm** in AI Plateau and only uneasy in Steady Disruption, worrying for office colleagues.
In the AGI pictures she dates her job's end to the **robot arrival** and plans a house and a repair trade.
More warning time lets her **save steadily** instead of buying a house in a rush.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because five years is too short to buy a house and retrain.
whatWouldHelp: She wants Hartley's to **fund retraining** before buying robot lorries.
She wants **banks to keep lending** to drivers when automation is in the news.
